M2 — Directional asymmetry of switching thresholds for a single rotor.
Observation: pair_A rotor 1, mount L=0, other rotor at −: up threshold +7.3 cm, down −7.1 cm; with other at +: up +7.3, down −7.1. Rotor 2, L=0: up 3.5 (other −1), down 0.1 (other −1); up 3.5 (other +1), down 0.1 (other +1). So asymmetric: |up| ≠ |down| notably for rotor 2 (3.5 vs 0.1), meaning the energy landscape is tilted/asymmetric (biased well depths) — not a symmetric double well.
Conditions: other rotor clamped at a stop; quasistatic drive; hard stops; ±0.1 cm.
Expectation: For a symmetric bistable element, |up| = |down|; asymmetry implies a bias (gravity, rest-length preload, geometry offset, stop positions), and the loop is "shifted" like a Preisach hysteron with asymmetric thresholds (α ≠ −β).
Existing explanations: Preisach/play operator admits asymmetric thresholds; asymmetric energy landscapes in bistable arches produce nonreciprocal / one-way transition waves (S2); prestress/tilt.
Unknowns: source of bias (gravity torque of the bar? rest lengths? mount offsets [0, −1.9]); whether threshold asymmetry is a property of the element or of the clamp/stops; no error bars; ±0.1 cm resolution; hysteresis of the drive train.

M3 — Coupling-attachment-distance dependence (mount L sweep in pair_A).
Observation: For rotor 1 with other at +, up threshold decreases from 7.3 (L=0) to 7.1, 5.9, 4.3 as L goes 0, 1.577, 3.154, 4.731 cm; with other at −, up goes 7.3, 7.1, 6.5, 5.5. Rotor 2 with other at +: up 3.5, 3.1, 2.1, 0.5; down 0.1, −0.1, −0.9, −1.7. Rotor 2 with other at −: up 3.5,3.5,3.9,4.9; down 0.1,0.3,1.1,2.7.
So the sign of the change with L depends on other_state and rotor: rotor 1's threshold decreases with L whatever other_state; rotor 2's increases when other=−1 and decreases when other=+1. That's a striking, concrete pattern. Effective coupling torque ∝ k_coupling * (moment arm factor of L) * sin difference; symmetric: threshold shift should change sign with other_state. Rotor 1 shows decrease in both cases (with other=+ stronger). Hmm interesting.
Expectation: the coupling spring exerts a torque whose magnitude grows with attachment distance L (moment arm ~ L·sinθ), so the threshold shift should scale with L and flip sign when the other rotor's state flips (because the coupling force direction reverses). Observed: sign flip for rotor 2 (yes: + with other=−1, − with other=+1), but not for rotor 1 (decreases in both, weaker when other=−1). That's an anomaly worth flagging — a good "unknown".
Existing explanations: spring torque linear in extension; geometry (x_mount_offsets [0, −1.9]); parallel vs crossed coupling; finite angle effects; stop-limited geometry.
Unknowns: exact coupling attachment points (x offsets ±1.9), whether rotor 1's coupling attachment is off-center producing a torque that does not reverse; whether the L=0 case still has coupling (spring at pivot → no torque? yet thresholds at L=0 differ by other_state? rotor1 up=7.3 both; rotor2 same 3.5 both — at L=0 the other state has no effect, consistent with zero moment arm).

So at L=0 thresholds are identical for other_state ±1 (rotor1 7.3/7.3, rotor2 3.5/3.5 for up; down −7.1/−7.1 and 0.1/0.1). Great: confirms zero coupling moment arm at L=0. Then as L increases, coupling matters. For rotor 1 the other=+ case changes more strongly than other=−. For rotor 2 signs flip.

M4 — Crossed vs parallel coupling topology (pair_A vs pair_B).
Observation: pair_B rotor 2 at L=4.7 cm: up threshold 24.9 (other −1) and 30.7 (other +1); down 2.1 and 7.3. pair_A rotor 2 at L=4.7: up 4.9 / 0.5; down 2.7 / −1.7. So pair_B thresholds are ~5-10× larger, and the ordering as a function of other_state reverses (pair_B: other=+ gives larger up threshold; pair_A: other=+ gives smaller). Also pair_B all springs identical k=0.19, rest 4.1 (stiffer drive springs than pair_A's 0.19? same driving k 0.19; but coupling 0.07 in pair_A vs 0.19 in pair_B). So pair_B has stiffer coupling springs (0.19 vs 0.07 N/cm) plus crossed geometry → much larger threshold and opposite sign pattern.
Expectation: stronger coupling → larger threshold shifts; crossed geometry flips the sign of the coupling torque.
Unknowns: exact crossed geometry; whether threshold values > drive range (30.7 cm vs drive?) are reachable; whether pair_B's geometry differs also in mount offsets (−8.1, −16.4) and stop angles (±18.3, ±38.8); no L sweep in pair_B (single L=4.7).

M5 — Multi-rotor network event sequence (network_C).
Observation: 16 ordered events forming exactly two identical 8-event cycles; each successive event changes exactly one rotor state; recorded drive positions repeat exactly between cycles (4.5, 5.8, 5.8, −4.3, −5.1, −5.1, 5.9, −3.3), including consecutive equal drive values (5.8 twice, −5.1 twice) where ordering is preserved but no timestamps.
Expectation: in a network of coupled hysterons, a quasistatic cyclic drive returns to the same state at the same drive value if the sequence is return-point-memory (Preisach-like) and no rearrangement/wear; the number of intermediate states depends on the ordering of individual thresholds; sequential single-flip events (no avalanche) is expected when coupling is weak relative to threshold spread, whereas strong coupling gives avalanches/collective flips.
Existing explanations: hysteron-network picture where the global state sequence is determined by the set of thresholds and interactions (Preisach superposition when non-interacting); transition waves in coupled bistable lattices when elements are strongly coupled (S1, S2).
Unknowns: reversal positions not recorded (protocol says do not infer from extrema); whether the drive is a symmetric triangle wave; whether the sequence contains hidden simultaneous flips (two events at same drive could be simultaneous-ish); the exact connectivity and stop angles of network_C; whether all 8 events occur within one half-cycle or across the full cycle; whether the same state can be reached at different drive values.

Actually can we infer something about reversal? At event 8 state ---+ at drive −3.3 then event 9 returns to -+-+ at +4.5 → so the reversal happened somewhere below −3.3 and drive went up to +4.5. Not to be inferred per protocol, fine.

M6 (optional) — Threshold vs drive-rate/direction and "congruency" assumption: the up/down thresholds measured with other rotor clamped provide the hysteron's α/β; the Preisach model would predict network behavior as a weighted superposition of these single-element operators, assuming no interaction beyond the fixed-state condition. But clamping the other rotor at a stop is not the same as it being free — interactions during a joint transition are inaccessible; interactions generally break congruency/wiping-out. This is a "theory's successful range" material: can state as an open situation about whether pair_A's measured single-element thresholds suffice to predict network_C's 8-event cycle.
